content.title: DISH blackout Update: When will local channels come back? How to watch now
content.text: Find out why DISH viewers still can't access local TV and the best alternatives right now. (photo credit: Business Wire 2017 via AP)Copyright Business Wire 2017 via APIf you purchase a product through a link on our site, we may receive compensation.DISH Network subscribers across the U.S. are still navigating widespread local‑channel blackouts more than a month after a high‑profile carriage dispute with Gray Media removed hundreds of broadcast stations from the satellite provider’s lineup. What began as a contract standoff in early March has become one of the largest local TV disruptions in recent years, cutting off access to daily news, live sports, breaking weather coverage and primetime network favorites for millions of households.How DISH customers can still watch ABC, CBS, FOX, NBC and moreWhile negotiations remain unresolved, DISH subscribers have several reliable, safe alternatives to keep up with network programming:Live TV streaming servicesFubo – Offers local affiliates in many markets, a robust sports lineup, and a free trial with up to $30 in first‑month discounts DIRECTV – Includes most major broadcast networks, with a free trial and up to $40 off the first month for new customers Sling TV – Lower‑cost option that includes flexible streaming passes, and FOX and NBC in select markets via Sling Blue Network streaming platformsPeacock – Streams NBC programming, live sports and news starting at a low monthly starting rateParamount+ – Provides live CBS streams (Premium tier) plus on‑demand content from CBS and SHOWTIMEDisney+ and Hulu Bundle – A cost‑effective way to access ABC‑owned content, current‑season episodes and next‑day network shows What started the DISH–Gray Media blackout?The disruption began on March 10, 2026, when retransmission consent negotiations between DISH and Gray Media failed just ahead of a contract renewal deadline. When no agreement was in place, 226 Gray Media‑owned and operated stations across 113 markets were removed from DISH’s service nationwide.Affected stations include local affiliates of ABC, CBS, FOX, NBC, The CW, MyNetworkTV, and Telemundo, leaving viewers without familiar local newscasts and marquee programming ranging from major network dramas to live professional and collegiate sports.Why negotiations broke downAt the center of the dispute are retransmission consent fees — payments that pay-TV providers make to carry local broadcast channels.DISH’s position: DISH says Gray Media demanded substantial fee increases that would ultimately raise customers’ monthly bills. The satellite provider also claims Gray introduced late‑stage conditions involving stations it does not yet own, leaving little time to finalize a deal before the deadline. Gray Media’s position: Gray Media maintains that DISH insisted on what it describes as a “materially adverse” contractual provision that is not present in its other distribution agreements. Gray also argues that DISH failed to negotiate in good faith under FCC retransmission rules, though details of the disputed fees have not been publicly disclosed.Industry analysts note that although Gray Media historically resolves disputes quickly, this standoff appears more entrenched, raising the possibility of a longer‑than‑average blackout.Current status As of mid‑April, there is still no announced restoration date for the missing channels. Both companies say they remain open to negotiations, but no public progress has been reported since early April. Neither DISH nor Gray Media has formally petitioned the FCC, though that option remains available if talks continue to stall.What to expect nextHistorically, most retransmission disputes end quietly once both sides reach a compromise behind closed doors. However, with both DISH and Gray Media describing the other’s demands as unprecedented, this blackout could continue longer than usual without regulatory pressure or shifting market conditions.
